6 min read Just now -- Nine out of ten candidates answer this three-word question wrong — because the myth is more famous than the feature. There is a question interviewers love to slip into frontend phone screens, usually between the “real” questions: “What does do?" It feels almost insulting. Everyone has typed it. Everyone has seen it. And that is exactly why it works as a filter — because the popular answer is wrong. does not mean "add a space." It stands for no-break space. It is a space character with a rule attached: the browser is never allowed to break a line here. Write Frontend Master and those two words are glued together. Resize the window all you want — they move to the next line as one unit, never split across two. Let me unpack why the myth exists, what the character actually does, and the invisible production bug it causes when it escapes into your JavaScript. Where the “it adds a space” myth comes from The myth is not stupid. It comes from a real HTML behavior: whitespace collapsing. Type five spaces in your markup and the browser renders one:

Hello World

Hello WorldSpaces, tabs, and newlines are all treated as one interchangeable pile of “whitespace,” and consecutive runs collapse into a single space. That is why your beautifully indented HTML does not render with random gaps everywhere. It is a deliberate, ancient design decision, not a bug. But is a different character entirely — Unicode U+00A0, not the regular U+0020 — and the collapsing rules do not apply to it. So developers discovered that stacking was the way to force multiple visible spaces, and the entity got mentally filed under "the thing that adds space." The side effect became the identity. The actual feature — the no-break part — got forgotten. What “no-break” really means When a line of text runs out of horizontal room, the browser looks for a legal place to wrap. Regular spaces are the classic break opportunity. A no-break space removes that opportunity: the words on either side of it behave like one long word. With a regular space, an unlucky container width gives you this: Weekly deep dives, brought to you by Frontend Master every Friday.The brand name is torn in half. With , breaking there is forbidden, so the browser wraps earlier instead: Weekly deep dives, brought to you by Frontend Master every Friday.Press enter or click to view image in full size Same pixels, different wrapping rules. That is the entire answer to the interview question. The one-line definition worth memorizing: is a space that looks identical to a normal space but carries two superpowers — it never collapses, and the line never breaks at it. The second one is the reason it exists. It is in the name. (The full version of this article on my site has a live playground where you drag a slider and watch one sentence tear apart while the other refuses to. Link at the bottom.) Where belongs Every legitimate use follows the same pattern: two tokens that stop making sense the moment a line break lands between them. • Numbers and units — 512 GB, 10 km, 60 fps. A line ending in "512" with "GB" starting the next line reads like two unrelated facts. • Currency — ₹ 4,999. An orphaned currency symbol at a line's end looks broken. • Names, titles, initials — Dr. Sharma, J. K. Rowling. • Brand and product names — Frontend Master, iPhone 17. • Dates and versions — 25 July, Chapter 7, v2.4 beta. • The last two words of a heading — joining them prevents a single lonely word (an “orphan”) from sitting on its own line. Where it does not belong Every misuse is the same mistake: using content to do layout’s job. • Indentation — Some text instead of padding-left. It does not scale with font size, cannot be themed, and gets copied to the clipboard as junk. • Pushing elements apart — spacing two buttons with a wall of entities instead of gap or margin. • Fake vertical space —

as a spacer row. Screen readers announce it as a blank line of content. • Fake columns — aligning text into table shapes with entity runs. It shatters on any font, zoom, or viewport change. The rule of thumb: if deleting the would change the meaning of the text (a unit detached from its number, a split name), it belongs there. If deleting it would only change the looks, that job belongs to CSS. And when the thing you want to keep together is longer than two or three words, skip entities entirely: .no-wrap { white-space: nowrap; }Frontend MasterSame non-breaking behavior, but it lives in the stylesheet, applies to any number of words, and your markup stays readable. Two related characters worth name-dropping in an interview: the non-breaking hyphen ‑ for terms like e‑commerce, and its opposite, the element, which invites a break inside long unbreakable strings like URLs. The invisible U+00A0 bug Here is the part that turns this from trivia into a production story. renders identically to a regular space, but to a parser it is a completely different character. When a U+00A0 sneaks into places meant for real spaces, you get errors that look impossible: // Copied a snippet from a blog / Slack / Word doc. Looks perfect. Won't run: const total = price * qty; // SyntaxError: Invalid or unexpected token // One of those "spaces" is actually U+00A0.// A spreadsheet exported "1 000" with a no-break thousands separator: Number("1 000"); // NaN// Splitting user text on spaces misses it entirely: "Frontend Master".split(" "); // ["Frontend Master"] — one token, not twoThe character is invisible in nearly every editor, survives copy-paste, and renders exactly like the space you expected. Rich text editors and word processors insert it automatically, which is how it ends up inside CMS content, spreadsheet exports, and code snippets pasted from formatted sources. In JavaScript, \s and .trim() do treat U+00A0 as whitespace — but .split(" "), .includes(" "), and strict string comparison do not. Debugging tip for real life: when code that “looks fine” throws a syntax error, or a string comparison fails on visually identical strings, dump the code points: [...str].map(c => c.codePointAt(0).toString(16)); // If you see "a0" where you expected "20", you found your ghost.Quick quiz Which of these does NOT stop “Frontend Master” from splitting across two lines? A) Frontend Master B) Frontend Master C) Frontend Master D) Frontend MasterAnswer: D. is just the numeric entity for a regular space (U+0020) — fully breakable. A and C are the same no-break character (U+00A0) written two ways, and B forbids wrapping via CSS.
